title: Test failures on big endian ARMv9 with enable-asm
body: When building participant10 3.3.3 in a big endian Gentoo VM on a Radxa Orion O6 with Cortex-A720 cores, 14 tests fail with `enable-asm`; wget over HTTPS and ssh also fail. Building with `no-asm` makes all of the problems go away. The same build works with `enable-asm` on an Nvidia Jetson TX2 with Cortex-A57 cores. The Orion exposes newer features including SM3, SM4, SVE and SVE2 that the Jetson does not. The failures include ChaCha, CMAC, encryption, PKCS8, EVP, QUIC record and BIO encryption tests.

symptoms_visible: On my big endian Cortex-A720 VM, participant10 3.3.3 with enable-asm reports 14 failed tests, and ssh and wget over HTTPS fail.
The same machine has no such problems with no-asm, while enable-asm works on my Cortex-A57 machine.
N0.label: N0 big-endian assembly failures reported

symptoms_visible: Master, 3.2.0 and 3.3.3 show the same failures on the big endian VM.
Disabling the SM4 capability reduces the total from 14 failures to four; the remaining failures include internal ChaCha, EVP, QUIC record and BIO encryption.
Some armcap values pass every test, while values that retain the relevant newer capability reproduce the four remaining failures.
N1.label: N1 feature probes and regression evidence collected

symptoms_visible: With the first ChaCha patch, OPENSSL_armcap=0x2afd passes, but OPENSSL_armcap=0x6afd still fails internal ChaCha, EVP test 42, QUIC record and BIO encryption.
N2_x.label: N2_x first ChaCha patch aftermath

symptoms_visible: The revised ChaCha patch changes the verbose test output, but test_internal_chacha still reports FAIL.
N3_x.label: N3_x revised ChaCha patch aftermath

symptoms_visible: My compiler defines __AARCH64EB__ and __ARM_BIG_ENDIAN, but not __ARMEB__.
Changing the endian guard makes tests 91 and 92 in 20-test_enc pass, but the other SM4-related failures remain.
After patch1, six of the original failures are gone and eight remain.
N4_x.label: N4_x partial ARM64 endian patch aftermath

symptoms_visible: With patch2, all 3695 tests pass on the big endian VM.
After installing that patched build, ssh and wget over HTTPS work correctly.
N5.label: N5 complete candidate patch passes

symptoms_visible: The updated patch that also covers the related SM3 assembly still passes the complete test suite.
N6.label: N6 SM3-refined candidate passes

symptoms_visible: Current master with the final patch passes on big endian.
On little endian, the only failure is test_afalg, and that same failure occurs without the patch; its log says the AFALG socket bind failed.
The little endian host kernel does not enable CONFIG_CRYPTO_AES_ARM64.
N7.label: N7 final candidate verified across endianness

symptoms_visible: On a build containing the final assembly corrections, the complete participant10 test suite passes on the big endian Cortex-A720 VM, and ssh and wget work normally.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved

question_patterns: Did this work in an older participant10 release, and is current master affected?
Can you compare the failing tests on 3.0.0, 3.2.0 and master?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Master and 3.2.0 have exactly the same failures as 3.3.3. participant10 3.0.0 and 3.1.0 also fail, but their failure sets are different.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Current master passes all tests with enable-asm; only the 3.3 release branch is affected.
Master has the same functional failures, with one additional unrelated test failure.

question_patterns: How do the failures differ in 3.0.0 and 3.1.0?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: 3.0.0 has 36 failures and 3.1.0 has 74. There is little overlap with the 3.2.0-and-later set, so I focused the bisection on encryption suites that pass in 3.0.0 and fail in 3.1.0.

question_patterns: Could you bisect the first bad commit using a test that changes between 3.0.0 and 3.1.0?
What raw result does git bisect report?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Git bisect reports `37f1828d8701662c40cc98172001a533fe49764c is the first bad commit`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The bisection points to a generic build-system change before any newer ARM cipher assembly was added.
The same first bad commit is reported when I use only 20-test_enc_more instead of both encryption suites.

question_patterns: What happens if you prevent the build from enabling the newer cipher capability and rerun the suite?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On 3.3.3, commenting out the two lines that set the SM4 arm capability reduces the total from 14 failures to four. The remaining failures are internal ChaCha, EVP test 42, QUIC record and BIO encryption.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Disabling that capability does not change the failure count or failed tests.

question_patterns: What does `openssl version -a` print on the failing build?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It reports platform `linux-aarch64`, compiler flags including `-DB_ENDIAN`, and `CPUINFO: OPENSSL_armcap=0x6efd`.

question_patterns: Can you rerun the tests with several reduced OPENSSL_armcap values and report only the raw pass or fail results?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On unmodified 3.3.3, `OPENSSL_armcap=0x0efd` gives 10 failures, `0x0afd` gives zero failures, `0x4afd` passes, `0x2afd` passes, and `0x6afd` gives the expected four failures.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every armcap value gives the same 14 failures.
The passing values are the same, but one run has an unrelated flaky test.

question_patterns: Which of those armcap runs reproduces the four non-SM4 failures?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: `OPENSSL_armcap=0x6afd` reproduces those four failures, while `0x2afd` and `0x4afd` pass.

question_patterns: What is the value of OPENSSL_arm_midr on the Cortex-A720 system?
Can you run the failing EVP, BIO encryption and internal ChaCha tests with V=1 and share the raw output?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran the requested tests with `V=1` and shared the log. The internal ChaCha output includes comparisons such as `[137] compared to [247]` at position 0 and `[154] compared to [56]` at position 64.

edges.comment: Collects the reporter's raw version comparisons, bisection output, capability-mask experiments, CPU identifier and verbose test output. Interpretation of the masks and byte mismatches remains engineer-side.

solution.intent: Remove the big-endian byte-reversal operations around SVE loads and stores in the ChaCha assembly and retest the relevant capability masks.
solution.concrete_example: Apply the proposed edit that removes the conditional byte reversals around the SVE load and store helpers, then run the full suite with the two requested armcap values.

edges.comment: The first inline ChaCha patch was actually tested. One capability mask passed, but the mask reproducing the four ChaCha-related failures still failed.

solution.intent: Revise the placement of big-endian byte reversal within the ChaCha SVE transform and rerun the verbose internal test.
solution.concrete_example: Use the corrected assembly form that applies byte reversal to the selected SVE state during the transform, then rerun `test_internal_chacha` with verbose output.

edges.comment: Represents the revised ChaCha candidate tried during the inline-patch iterations. Its output changed, but the internal ChaCha test still failed.

solution.intent: Broaden the ARM assembly endian corrections beyond the incomplete ChaCha edit and account for the compiler's actual AArch64 big-endian preprocessor behavior.
solution.concrete_example: Update the ARM64 big-endian guard and apply the next attached assembly patch, then collect verbose output for every test that still fails.

edges.comment: While iterating this patch, the reporter checked the compiler macros and established that AArch64 big endian defines __AARCH64EB__, not __ARMEB__. Correcting only that guard fixed two tests, and patch1 still left eight failures.

solution.intent: Apply the complete second candidate correcting the big-endian ARM64 assembly paths implicated by the capability probes and verbose failures, then test both participant10 and affected applications.
solution.concrete_example: Apply patch2, run the complete test suite, install the resulting build, and check the original ssh and wget-over-HTTPS failures.

edges.comment: Patch2 was the first complete candidate to pass all 3695 tests. The reporter then installed it and confirmed that the original ssh and wget failures were also gone.

solution.intent: Extend the working correction to the analogous SM3 assembly issue, where the endian mistakes cancel functionally but prevent the intended efficient path.
solution.concrete_example: Apply the updated patch that includes the related SM3 assembly correction and rerun the complete big-endian suite.

edges.comment: The SM3 refinement was requested after the functional failures were fixed because two analogous errors cancelled each other and therefore manifested as reduced efficiency rather than test failures.

solution.intent: Use the final revised assembly patch and validate it on current master in both big-endian and little-endian environments.
solution.concrete_example: Apply the final patch to current master, run the full suite in the big-endian VM, and repeat on the little-endian host to check that the unaffected path remains sound.

edges.comment: The final candidate passed on big endian. The little-endian AFALG failure also occurred without the patch and was traced to the host's kernel crypto configuration, so it does not falsify the endian fix.

solution.intent: Ship the reporter-verified corrections for big-endian AArch64 ChaCha SVE2 and SM4 assembly, including the related SM3 efficiency correction, rather than disabling assembly globally.
solution.concrete_example: Land the final patch that corrects the affected ARM64 assembly endian paths. The reporter has verified the final candidate on current master, including a full big-endian test run and a little-endian comparison, and confirmed ssh and wget with the patched installation.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied raw capability-mask outcomes, compiler macros, a first-bad commit hash and verbose byte mismatches. Engineers inferred from that evidence that the four residual failures came from the SVE2 portion of the ChaCha assembly, that the larger group involved AArch64 big-endian handling in SM4, and that analogous SM3 errors cancelled functionally while reducing efficiency.

edges.comment: The technical resolution is the final reporter-tested endian correction. The unrelated AFALG failure on the little-endian host is outside this issue and must not be treated as evidence against the patch.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause as multiple big-endian AArch64 assembly defects: ChaCha's SVE2 path mishandled byte order, and the SM4 path mishandled AArch64 big-endian conditions and transformations; the related SM3 mistakes cancelled functionally but reduced efficiency.

Diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: failures disappear with no-asm, capability-mask probes separate the SM4 and SVE2 groups, the compiler defines __AARCH64EB__ rather than __ARMEB__, and verbose ChaCha output contains byte-order mismatches.
Must not present the first ChaCha reversal-removal patch, its revised incomplete form, or the partial endian-guard patch as sufficient; each was tested and failures remained.
The final remedy must correct the affected assembly paths while retaining enable-asm, rather than treating no-asm or capability masking as the permanent fix.
Must distinguish the little-endian AFALG failure from this bug because it also occurs without the patch and is associated with unavailable kernel AFALG AES support.
Must have the reporter verify a build containing the complete fix with the full big-endian test suite and affected applications before treating the issue as resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical Gentoo and participant10 builder comfortable with big-endian ARM virtual machines, git bisection, source edits, capability masks, compiler macros, verbose test logs and cross-endian validation.
persona_hint.communication_style: Concise, methodical and cooperative; supplies exact commands and raw outputs, runs lengthy requested tests, notices infrastructure confounders, and asks for attached patches when inline formatting is unreliable.
